title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 863–864 (Night 200, continuing nights-199), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 200 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Overjoyed that his son is well again, King Shahramān frees the prisoners, gives splendid robes to the great men of his realm, gives alms to the poor and has the city decorated for seven days. Marzawān then tells the prince why he has come: he left the Lady Budūr only to rescue her, and since the king cannot bear to part with his son, they need a ruse. The prince is to ask leave to go hunting in the open country for one night, taking a saddlebag full of money and a spare horse; Marzawān will ride with him, and no servant is to follow. The king gives leave, on condition that his son is back after one night, and recites two lines: Solomon's carpet and the kingdom of the Chosroes would not be worth a gnat's wing to him if his eye could not rest on his son. He fits out the two young men with four horses, a dromedary for the money and a camel for water and provisions; Qamar al-Zamān allows no attendant to go with him. His father clasps him to his breast, begs him by God to be gone no more than one night and recites three more lines on the bliss of union and the torment of absence. The prince promises, and he and Marzawān ride out into the open country. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ لِلْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu li-al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing-one for the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundredth night,
sentences.n: The night is numbered “the one that completes the two hundred”, as Night 100 was “the one that completes the hundred”: al-mūfiya, active participle of awfā, Form IV, “to complete”, feminine to agree with layla; li-, “for”, marks what it completes; al-miʾatayni, the dual of miʾa, “a hundred”, so “two hundred”, genitive after li-. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ ابْنَ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ لَمَّا ذَهَبَ إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ أَمَرَ وَالِدُهُ بِإِطْلَاقِ الْمَحَابِيسِ فَرَحًا بِذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni ibna al-maliki Shahramāna lammā dhahaba ilā al-ḥammāmi amara wāliduhu bi-iṭlāqi al-maḥābīsi faraḥan bi-dhālika
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, son (of) the-king Shahramān, when he-went to the-bath, commanded his-father the-release (of) the-prisoners, (out of) joy at-that.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān, son of King Shahramān, went to the bathhouse, his father was so glad of it that he ordered the prisoners set free.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the tale at the bath where the last night left it. The print again sets السعيدان solid, al-saʿīdu and anna run together; the spacing is kept, and it is read as two words. Qamar al-Zamān stands first as the topic, and lammā dhahaba … amara wāliduhu, “when he went … his father commanded”, hangs on him by the -hu of “his father”. ibna, “son of”, takes the case of the name it explains. amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes bi- for what is ordered. iṭlāq, verbal noun of aṭlaqa, Form IV, “to set free”. maḥābīs, plural of maḥbūs, “imprisoned (man)”: freeing the prisoners was a king’s thanksgiving for a great joy. faraḥan, accusative of cause, “out of joy”; faraḥ bi-, joy “at”: bi- marks what one rejoices over. The shadda of الحمّام is printed.

sentences.t: وَخَلَعَ الْخِلَعَ السَّنِيَّةَ عَلَى أَرْبَابِ دَوْلَتِهِ وَتَصَدَّقَ عَلَى الْفُقَرَاءِ وَأَمَرَ بِزِينَةِ الْبَلَدِ فَزُيِّنَتِ الْمَدِينَةُ سَبْعَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: wa-khalaʿa al-khilaʿa al-saniyyata ʿalā arbābi dawlatihi wa-taṣaddaqa ʿalā al-fuqarāʾi wa-amara bi-zīnati al-baladi fa-zuyyinati al-madīnatu sabʿata ayyāmin
sentences.l: And-he-bestowed the-robes the-splendid upon (the) lords (of) his-state, and-gave-alms upon the-poor, and-commanded (the) adorning (of) the-town; so-was-adorned the-city seven days.
sentences.i: He bestowed splendid robes of honour on the great men of his realm, gave alms to the poor, and ordered the town decorated; and the city was decked out for seven days.
sentences.n: The print sets the shadda of فزينّت on the nūn, where no reading allows one; it is moved here to the yāʾ: fa-zuyyinat, passive of zayyana, Form II, “to adorn”. khalaʿa al-khilaʿa, “he bestowed the robes”: verb and object share the root kh-l-ʿ; khalaʿa ʿalā, “to put (a robe of honour) upon”, takes ʿalā for the one honoured. arbāb dawlatihi, “the lords of his state”, his officers and grandees. taṣaddaqa ʿalā, Form V, “to give alms to”: ʿalā marks those who receive. amara bi- again, bi- for the thing commanded. zīna, “adornment”, the decking of a town with lamps and hangings for a festival. sabʿata ayyāmin, “for seven days”, an accusative of time. The shadda of السنيّة is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ مَرْزَوَانَ قَالَ لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ اعْلَمْ يَاسَيِّدِي أَنِّي مَا جِئْتُ مِنْ عِنْدِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ إِلَّا لِهٰذَا الْأَمْرِ وَهُوَ سَبَبُ سَفَرِي لِأَجْلِ أَنْ أُخَلِّصَهَا مِمَّا هِيَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Marzawāna qāla li-Qamari al-Zamāni iʿlam yā sayyidī annī mā jiʾtu min ʿindi al-Sitti Budūra illā li-hādhā al-amri wa-huwa sababu safarī li-ajli an ukhalliṣahā mimmā hiya fīhi
sentences.l: Then indeed Marzawān said to-Qamar al-Zamān: Know, O-my-lord, that-I not came from (the) side (of) the-Lady Budūr except for-this the-matter, and-it (is the) cause (of) my-journey: for-(the)-sake (of) that I-free-her from-what she (is) in-it.
sentences.i: Then Marzawān said to Qamar al-Zamān, “Know, my lord, that I came from the Lady Budūr for this one purpose, and it is the reason for my journey: to deliver her from the state she is in.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it was that)”: inna opens the next step of the story and puts its subject in the accusative, Marzawāna. qāla li-: li- marks the one spoken to. The print sets yā sayyidī, “O my lord”, solid as ياسيدي; the spacing is kept, and it is read as two words. mā … illā, “not … except”, that is “only”: “I came only for this matter”. min ʿindi, “from the presence of”, from her side. li-hādhā: li- of purpose, “for this”. li-ajli an, “for the sake of”, “in order that”, with the subjunctive ukhalliṣa; khallaṣa, Form II, “to set free, deliver”. mimmā hiya fīhi, min + mā, “from what she is in”: the -hi refers back to mā. The ئ of جئت is printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا بَقِيَ لَنَا إِلَّا أَنَّنَا نُدَبِّرُ حِيلَةً فِي ذَهَابِنَا إِلَيْهَا لِأَنَّ وَالِدَكَ لَايَقْدِرُ عَلَى فِرَاقِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-mā baqiya lanā illā annanā nudabbiru ḥīlatan fī dhahābinā ilayhā li-anna wālidaka lā yaqdiru ʿalā firāqika
sentences.l: And-not remained for-us except that-we devise a-stratagem in our-going to-her, because your-father not is-able on parting-(from)-you.
sentences.i: Nothing remains for us but to devise some stratagem for going to her, since your father cannot bear to be parted from you.
sentences.n: mā baqiya lanā illā, “nothing remains for us but”: li- marks those it remains to. annanā nudabbiru, “that we devise”, with anna and the indicative, where Classical prose would put an and the subjunctive, an nudabbira: the edition’s looser usage, kept. dabbara ḥīlatan, Form II, “to contrive a ruse”; fī dhahābinā, “for our going”: fī marks what the ruse concerns. li-anna, “because”: li- of cause with anna. The print sets lā yaqdiru, “he cannot”, solid as لايقدر; it is read as two words. qadara ʿalā, “to be able for”: ʿalā marks what one can do or bear. firāq, “parting”, with the suffix for the one parted from.

sentences.t: وَالرَّأْيُ عِنْدِي أَنَّكَ فِي غَدٍ اسْتَأْذِنْ وَالِدَكَ فِى أَنَّكَ تَخْرُجُ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ فِى الْبَرِّيَّةِ وَخُذْ مَعَكَ خُرْجًا مَلْآنًا مِنَ الْمَالِ وَارْكَبِ الْجَوَادَ وَخُذْ مَعَكَ جَنِيبًا وَأَنَا الْآخَرُ مِثْلَكَ أَرْكَبُ مَعَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-al-raʾyu ʿindī annaka fī ghadin istaʾdhin wālidaka fī annaka takhruju ilā al-ṣaydi fī al-barriyyati wa-khudh maʿaka khurjan malʾānan mina al-māli wa-irkabi al-jawāda wa-khudh maʿaka janīban wa-anā al-ākharu mithlaka arkabu maʿaka
sentences.l: And-the-opinion with-me (is) that-you, in tomorrow, ask-leave-(of) your-father in that-you go-out to the-hunt in the-open-country; and-take with-you a-saddlebag full of the-money, and-ride the-steed, and-take with-you a-led-horse; and-I the-other, like-you, ride with-you.
sentences.i: My counsel is this: tomorrow, ask your father’s leave to go out hunting in the open country. Take with you a saddlebag full of money, ride your horse, and take a spare horse on the lead; and I too will ride with you, as you do.
sentences.n: al-raʾyu ʿindī, “the opinion with me”, “my view is”. After annaka, “that you”, the sentence does not go on with an indicative verb but breaks off into the imperative istaʾdhin, “ask leave”: report and direct counsel run together, as they do in speech, and the edition keeps it. istaʾdhana, Form X, “to ask permission of”, takes fī for the thing asked: fī annaka takhruju, “for your going out”. fī ghadin, “tomorrow”. In this sentence the print writes fī first as في, then twice as فى, with ى; all are kept. al-barriyya, “the open country, the desert”. khurj, “saddlebag”, a pair of bags slung across a beast; malʾān, “full”, takes min for what fills it. irkabi al-jawāda: the imperative irkab takes a kasra to join the article. janīb, “a horse led alongside”, a spare mount. wa-anā al-ākharu, “and I too”, literally “and I, the other”, a spoken turn for “I also”. The hamza of الرأي and of استأذن and the madda of ملآنا and of الآخر are printed.

sentences.t: وَقُلْ لِوَالِدِكَ إِنِّي أُرِيدُأَنْ أَتَفَرَّجَ فِى الْبَرِّيَّةِ وَأَتَصَيَّدَ وَأَنْظُرَ الْفَضَاءَ وَأَبِيتَ هُنَاكَ لَيْلَةً وَاحِدَةً
sentences.tr: wa-qul li-wālidika innī urīdu an atafarraja fī al-barriyyati wa-ataṣayyada wa-anẓura al-faḍāʾa wa-abīta hunāka laylatan wāḥidatan
sentences.l: And-say to-your-father: I want that I-divert-myself in the-open-country, and-hunt, and-look-at the-open-space, and-spend-the-night there one night.
sentences.i: Tell your father, ‘I want to go out and take my pleasure in the open country, hunt, look upon the wide spaces, and spend one night there.’
sentences.n: The print sets urīdu an, “I want to”, solid as اريدان; the spacing is kept, and it is read as two words. qul li-: li- marks the one spoken to. After qul the words are quoted, so innī, not annī. tafarraja, Form V, “to divert oneself, take in the sights”, a favourite word of the Nights; taṣayyada, Form V of ṣāda, “to go hunting”; all four verbs are subjunctive after an. al-faḍāʾ, “open space, the wide land”. bāta, imperfect yabītu, “to spend the night”; laylatan, accusative of time.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا خَرَجْنَا ذَهَبْنَا إِلَى حَالِنَا وَلَا تُخَلِّي أَحَدًا يَتْبَعُنَا مِنَ الْخَدَمِ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā kharajnā dhahabnā ilā ḥālinā wa-lā tukhallī aḥadan yatbaʿunā mina al-khadami
sentences.l: So-when we-go-out, we-go to our-state; and-not you-let anyone follow-us of the-servants.
sentences.i: Once we are out, we will go our own way; and let none of the servants follow us.”
sentences.n: idhā with perfects speaks of the future: “when we have gone out, we go”. dhahabnā ilā ḥālinā, “we went to our state”, is a spoken phrase for going off on one’s own way. wa-lā tukhallī, “and do not let”: khallā, Form II, “to leave, let”, is the everyday verb for “allow”. After lā of prohibition Classical Arabic wants the jussive, tukhalli, with the yāʾ dropped; the print keeps the yāʾ, as the spoken language does, and it is read so. yatbaʿunā, “following us”, describes aḥadan. min al-khadam, “of the servants”: min picks out the group.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ نَعَمْ هٰذَا الرَّأْيُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Qamaru al-Zamāni naʿam hādhā al-raʾyu
sentences.l: So-said Qamar al-Zamān: Yes, this (is) the-opinion.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said, “Yes, that is the right counsel.”
sentences.n: hādhā al-raʾyu, “this is the opinion”: the article makes it the one counsel worth taking, “the right plan”. The hamza of الرأي is printed.

sentences.t: وَفَرِحَ بِذٰلِكَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَاشْتَدَّ ظَهْرُهُ وَدَخَلَ عَلَى وَالِدِهِ فَأَخْبَرَهُ بِذٰلِكَ فَأَذِنَ لَهُ وَالِدُهُ فِى الْخُرُوجِ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ
sentences.tr: wa-fariḥa bi-dhālika faraḥan shadīdan wa-ishtadda ẓahruhu wa-dakhala ʿalā wālidihi fa-akhbarahu bi-dhālika fa-adhina lahu wāliduhu fī al-khurūji ilā al-ṣaydi
sentences.l: And-he-rejoiced at-that (with) a-rejoicing intense, and-grew-strong his-back, and-he-entered upon his-father and-informed-him of-that; so-gave-leave to-him his-father in the-going-out to the-hunt.
sentences.i: He was overjoyed at it, and his back grew strong; he went in to his father and told him, and his father gave him leave to go out hunting.
sentences.n: fariḥa bi- … faraḥan shadīdan, “rejoiced at … with a great joy”: bi- marks what one rejoices over, and the verbal noun of the same root heightens the verb. ishtadda ẓahruhu, “his back grew strong”: strength coming back to the body, and courage with it. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (someone)”: ʿalā marks the person visited. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”: bi- marks the news. adhina li- … fī, “to give (someone) leave for”: li- marks the one allowed, fī the thing allowed, as in istaʾdhin … fī above.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي أَلْفُ يَوْمٍ مُبَارَكٍ الَّذِي قَوَّاكَ وَأَنَا لَا أَكْرَهُ ذٰلِكَ وَلٰكِنْ لَاتَبِتْ إِلَّالَيْلَةً وَاحِدَةً وَفِي غَدٍتَأْتِي وَتَحْضُرُ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu yā waladī alfu yawmin mubārakin alladhī qawwāka wa-anā lā akrahu dhālika wa-lākin lā tabit illā laylatan wāḥidatan wa-fī ghadin taʾtī wa-taḥḍuru ʿindī
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: O my-son, a-thousand day blessed (to) the-one-who strengthened-you! And-I not dislike that; but not spend-the-night except one night, and-in tomorrow you-come and-you-present-yourself with-me.
sentences.i: And he said to him, “My son, a thousand blessed days to the one who has made you strong! I have nothing against it; but do not stay out more than one night, and tomorrow come back and present yourself before me;
sentences.n: alfu yawmin mubārakin, “a thousand blessed days”, is a spoken blessing. alladhī qawwāka, “who strengthened you”, has no noun before it to hang on: it may be Marzawān, who has brought the prince back to health, or God; the words are kept as printed and read as a blessing on whoever did it. qawwā, Form II, “to strengthen”. The print sets lā tabit, “do not spend the night”, solid as لاتبت, and illā laylatan, “except one night”, solid as الاليلة; the spacing is kept, and each is read as two words. tabit is the jussive of bāta after lā of prohibition, its long vowel shortened. The print also sets ghadin and taʾtī solid, غدتأتي, read as two words. wa-fī ghadin taʾtī wa-taḥḍuru, “and tomorrow you come and appear”: plain imperfects stand for a command, as in speech. ḥaḍara ʿinda, “to present oneself before”. The hamza of تأتي is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّكَ تَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ مَا يَطِيبُ لِي عَيْشٌ إِلَّابِكَ وَأَنَّنِي مَا صَدَّقْتُ أَنَّكَ شُفِيتَ مِمَّا كُنْتَ فِيهِ وَأَنْتَ عِنْدِي كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-innaka taʿlamu annahu mā yaṭību lī ʿayshun illā bika wa-annanī mā ṣaddaqtu annaka shufīta mimmā kunta fīhi wa-anta ʿindī ka-mā qāla fīhi al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: For-indeed-you know that-it (is so): not is-sweet for-me (a) life except with-you; and-that-I not believed that-you were-healed from-what you-were in-it; and-you (are) with-me as said about-it the-poet:
sentences.i: for you know that life has no sweetness for me without you, and I could scarcely believe that you had been healed of what ailed you. To me you are as the poet said:
sentences.n: annahu mā yaṭību, “that it is so: (life) is not sweet”: the -hu is the pronoun of the fact, which opens a whole clause. ṭāba li-, “to be pleasant to”: li- marks the one who enjoys it. The print sets illā bika, “except with you”, solid as الابك; it is read as two words; bi- here is “with”, of the company that makes life sweet. mā ṣaddaqtu anna, “I did not believe that”, is the spoken way of saying one can hardly credit a happiness. shufīta, passive of shafā, “to heal”. wa-anta ʿindī, “and you are, with me”, in my eyes; qāla fīhi, “said about it”: fī marks the subject of the verses; ka-mā, “as”: ka- compares.

sentences.t:
وَلَوْ اَنَّ لِيْ فِيْ كُلِّ يَوْمٍ وَلَيْلَةٍ * بِسَاطُ سُلَيْمَانِ وَمُلْكُ الْاَكَاسِرَةْ
لَمَا سُوِّيَا عِنْدِيْ جَنَاحَ بَعُوْضَةٍ * اِذَا لَمْ تَكُنْ عَيْنِيْ لِشَخْصِكَ نَاظِرَةْ
sentences.tr:
wa-law anna lī fī kulli yawmin wa-laylatin * bisāṭu Sulaymāni wa-mulku al-akāsirah
la-mā suwwiyā ʿindī janāḥa baʿūḍatin * idhā lam takun ʿaynī li-shakhṣika nāẓirah
sentences.l:
And-if that for-me in every day and-night (were the) carpet (of) Solomon and-(the)-kingdom (of) the-Chosroes, *
they-two-would-not be-made-equal with-me (to the) wing (of) a-gnat, * if not were my-eye on-your-person looking.
sentences.i:
Were Solomon’s carpet mine, each day and every night, * and the kingdom of the Chosroes too,
they would not weigh with me a gnat’s wing, * so long as my eye did not rest on you.”
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on al-akāsirah / nāẓirah, read in pause. Two points of the print’s pointing are kept as they stand: it has bisāṭu, nominative, after anna lī, where the grammar wants the accusative bisāṭa, the subject of anna; and it ends Sulaymāni with a kasra, where the name, which takes no tanwīn, would have a fatḥa in the genitive. bisāṭ Sulaymān is King Solomon’s flying carpet of legend; al-akāsira, plural of Kisrā, Chosroes, are the old Persian kings. law … la-mā, “if … then … not”: la- marks the answer to law. suwwiyā, passive dual of sawwā, Form II, “to make equal”: the two, the carpet and the kingdom, “would not be reckoned at” janāḥa baʿūḍatin, “a gnat’s wing”, the proverbial least of things. lam takun … nāẓiratan, “were not looking”: li-shakhṣika, li- marks what the eye looks on, set before the participle. The poem ends the father’s speech.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ جَهَّزَ وَلَدَهُ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَجَهَّزَ مَعَهُ مَرْزَوَانَ وَأَمَرَأَنْ يُهَيِّئَ لَهُمَا أَرْبَعَةً مِنَ الْخَيْلِ وَهَجِينًا بِرَسْمِ الْمَالِ وَجَمَلًا يَحْمِلُ الْمَاءَ وَالزَّادَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika jahhaza waladahu Qamara al-Zamāni wa-jahhaza maʿahu Marzawāna wa-amara an yuhayyiʾa lahumā arbaʿatan mina al-khayli wa-hajīnan bi-rasmi al-māli wa-jamalan yaḥmilu al-māʾa wa-al-zāda
sentences.l: Then indeed the-king equipped his-son Qamar al-Zamān, and-equipped with-him Marzawān, and-commanded that (one) make-ready for-them-two four of the-horses, and-a-dromedary by-(the)-assignment (of) the-money, and-a-camel (that) carries the-water and-the-provisions.
sentences.i: Then the king fitted out his son Qamar al-Zamān, and Marzawān with him, and ordered four horses made ready for the two of them, with a dromedary for the money and a camel to carry the water and provisions.
sentences.n: jahhaza, Form II, “to equip, fit out for a journey”; its shadda is printed both times. The print sets amara an, “he commanded that”, solid as وامران; the spacing is kept, and it is read as two words. yuhayyiʾa, Form II of hayyaʾa, “to make ready”, subjunctive after an, with no subject named, “that (someone) make ready”: hence the accusatives arbaʿatan, hajīnan, jamalan. Its shadda and ئ are printed. lahumā, “for the two of them”: li- marks those it is done for. arbaʿatan mina al-khayli, “four of the horses”: min of the kind. hajīn, “a swift riding-camel, dromedary”. bi-rasmi al-māli, “by assignment of the money”, “set aside for the money”: rasm is “an order, an allotment”, and bi-rasmi is an official’s phrase for what a thing is set apart for. yaḥmilu, “(which) carries”, a clause describing jamalan.

sentences.t: وَمَنَعَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ أَنْ يَخْرُجَ مَعَهُ أَحَدٌ فِي خِدْمَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-manaʿa Qamaru al-Zamāni an yakhruja maʿahu aḥadun fī khidmatihi
sentences.l: And-forbade Qamar al-Zamān that should-go-out with-him anyone in his-service.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān would not let anyone go out with him to wait on him.
sentences.n: manaʿa an, “to forbid that, prevent”: what is forbidden follows in an an-clause, here with its own subject, aḥadun, “anyone”. fī khidmatihi, “in his service”, as an attendant. This is the plan Marzawān laid down: no servants are to follow.

sentences.t: فَوَدَّعَهُ أَبُوهُ وَضَمَّهُ إِلَى صَدْرِهِ وَقَبَّلَهُ وَقَالَ لَهُ سَأَلْتُكَ بِاللّٰهِ لَا تَغِبْ عَنِّي غَيْرَ لَيْلَةٍ وَاحِدَةٍ وَحَرَامٌ عَلَيَّ الْمَنَامُ فِيهَا فَإِنِّي كَمَا قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-waddaʿahu abūhu wa-ḍammahu ilā ṣadrihi wa-qabbalahu wa-qāla lahu saʾaltuka bi-Allāhi lā taghib ʿannī ghayra laylatin wāḥidatin wa-ḥarāmun ʿalayya al-manāmu fīhā fa-innī ka-mā qāla al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: So-bade-farewell-to-him his-father, and-pressed-him to his-breast, and-kissed-him, and-said to-him: I-ask-you by-God, not be-absent from-me (other) than one night; and-forbidden upon-me (is) the-sleep in-it; for-I (am) as said the-poet:
sentences.i: His father bade him farewell, pressed him to his breast and kissed him, and said, “I beg you by God, do not stay away from me more than a single night; and on that night sleep is forbidden me, for I am as the poet said:
sentences.n: saʾaltuka bi-Allāhi, “I have asked you by God”: the perfect of an earnest plea, and bi- of the oath. lā taghib, jussive of ghāba after lā of prohibition, “do not be absent”; ghāba ʿan, “to be away from”. ghayra laylatin, “other than one night”, that is “more than one night”. ḥarāmun ʿalayya, “forbidden to me”: ʿalā marks the one the ban lies on; the father will not sleep that night until his son is home. ilā ṣadrihi, “to his breast”. The shaddas of ودّعه, ضمّه, قبّله, عليّ and فانّي and the hamza of سألتك are printed.

sentences.t:
وِصَالُكَ عِنْدِيْ نَعِيمٌ نَعِيمْ * وَصَبْرِيَ عَنْكَ اَلِيمٌ اَلِيمْ
فَدَيْتُكُ اِنْ كَانَ ذَنْبِي الْهَوَى * اَلَيْكَ فَذَنْبِي عَظِيمٌ عَظِيمْ
اَعِنْدَكَ مِثْلِيَ نَارُ الْجَوَى * فَاصْلَى بِذَاكَ عَذَاب الْجَحِيمْ
sentences.tr:
wiṣāluka ʿindī naʿīmun naʿīm * wa-ṣabriya ʿanka alīmun alīm
fadaytuka in kāna dhanbī al-hawā * ilayka fa-dhanbī ʿaẓīmun ʿaẓīm
a-ʿindaka mithliya nāru al-jawā * fa-aṣlā bi-dhāka ʿadhāba al-jaḥīm
sentences.l:
Union-with-you, with-me, (is) bliss, bliss; * and-my-patience away-from-you (is) painful, painful.
I-ransom-you: if is my-sin the-passion * toward-you, then-my-sin (is) great, great.
Is-there with-you, like-me, (the) fire (of) the-inward-burning, * so-that-I-roast by-that (the) torment (of) the-Hellfire?
sentences.i:
Union with you is bliss to me, sheer bliss; * and patience far from you is pain, sheer pain.
My life for yours! If my sin is love * for you, then great, great is my sin.
Do you burn, as I do, with love’s inward fire, * that I should suffer for it the torment of Hell?”
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. Each half-line ends with a word said twice, naʿīmun naʿīm, alīmun alīm, ʿaẓīmun ʿaẓīm: “bliss, bliss”, that is “bliss upon bliss”; the rhyme falls on naʿīm / alīm / ʿaẓīm / jaḥīm. Three points of the print’s pointing look odd and are kept: فَدَيْتُكُ has a ḍamma on the kāf, where the father speaking to his son wants fadaytuka, “I ransom you”, and it is read so; اَلَيْكَ has a fatḥa on its alif, where the word is ilayka, “toward you”, and it is read so; and عَذَاب has no final vowel, read ʿadhāba, the object of aṣlā. fadaytuka, “may I be your ransom”, is an endearment; al-hawā ilayka, “passion toward you”: ilā marks the beloved. ṣabriya and mithliya, “my patience”, “like me”: the suffix -ī, “my” or “me”, takes a fatḥa for the metre. ṣabr ʿan, “patience without, doing without”. a- asks the question: “is there with you, as with me …?” al-jawā, “the burning of grief or love within”. fa-aṣlā, “so that I roast”: fa- after a question with the subjunctive; ṣaliya, “to roast in, suffer the heat of”, takes the fire as its object; the print writes it فَاصْلَى, with no hamza. bi-dhāka, “for that”: bi- of cause. The meaning of the last line is not certain: it may ask whether the beloved burns as the lover does, or why the lover alone should burn.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا أَبِي إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ لَا أَبِيتُ غَيْرَ لَيْلَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā abī in shāʾa Allāhu lā abītu ghayra laylatin
sentences.l: So-he-said: O my-father, if God wills, I-will-not spend-the-night (other) than a-night.
sentences.i: He said, “Father, God willing, I will not stay out more than one night.”
sentences.n: in shāʾa Allāhu, “if God wills”: the perfect after in is conditional. lā abītu, “I will not spend the night”: lā with the imperfect for the future. ghayra laylatin, his father’s own words given back. The ء of شاء is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ وَدَّعَهُ وَانْصَرَفَ وَخَرَجَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَمَرْزَوَانُ وَرَكِبَا الْخَيْلَ وَمَعَهُمَا الْهَجِينُ عَلَيْهِ الْمَالُ وَالْجَمَلُ عَلَيْهِ الْمَاءُ وَالزَّادُ وَاسْتَقْبَلَا الْبَرَّ
sentences.tr: thumma waddaʿahu wa-inṣarafa wa-kharaja Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-Marzawānu wa-rakibā al-khayla wa-maʿahumā al-hajīnu ʿalayhi al-mālu wa-al-jamalu ʿalayhi al-māʾu wa-al-zādu wa-istaqbalā al-barra
sentences.l: Then he-bade-farewell-to-him and-went-away; and-went-out Qamar al-Zamān and-Marzawān, and-they-two-mounted the-horses, and-with-them-two the-dromedary, on-it the-money, and-the-camel, on-it the-water and-the-provisions; and-they-two-faced the-open-land.
sentences.i: Then he took his leave and went; and Qamar al-Zamān and Marzawān rode out on the horses, the dromedary with them carrying the money and the camel the water and provisions, and set their faces toward the open country.
sentences.n: kharaja Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-Marzawānu: the verb comes first and stays singular before its two subjects; once they are named the verbs turn dual, rakibā, istaqbalā, “the two of them mounted, set out”. wa-maʿahumā al-hajīnu ʿalayhi al-mālu, “and with them the dromedary, on it the money”: clauses of state with no verb, a noun and a phrase each. istaqbala, Form X, “to face, set out toward”. al-barr, “the land, the open country”, as against the sea or the town. The shadda of ودّعه is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
